status: Draft from the mishnah and R. Kulp's commentary only (each item carries its mishnah number). Kehati outranks R. Kulp and has not been read yet. Definitions are provisional until AnyDaf's master glossary covers them.

principles.t: The public domain belongs to everyone: no one may leave objects or dangerous materials there. If someone breaks an object left there he is exempt, but if he is hurt, the owner pays for the injury.
Pouring water, hiding thorns or glass, or letting a thorn fence fall into the public domain makes one liable for the injury, even if he tried to keep it out of people's way.

What a person puts out in the public domain and damages with, anyone who comes first may take, yet he still pays for the injury it causes. Whoever takes possession of something (turning over dung) must see that it injures no one.
The one who stumbles pays for the injury he causes if he could have got up in time. If he could not, it is an accident and he is exempt.

Everyone has the right to walk, and the right to run, in the public domain. Collisions where both have that right carry no liability; who pays depends on who was in front, a sudden stop, or a warning.
A livelihood may not damage others: one who splits wood is liable for any injury he causes, whichever domain either is in.
When two oxen or people hurt each other, the payment is for the greater hurt: half damages for a harmless ox, full damages for an attested danger or a person.

The same injury can bind the owner of the ox but not the person, and the reverse (embarrassment, a slave's eye, parents, fire on Shabbat). A person liable for death and money gets only the death penalty.
The burden of proof is on the one who wants payment. Without positive proof the defendant is exempt; two oxen with one owner make that owner liable.

terms.def: The street and other common ground. The sages considered it to belong to everyone, so no one may place dangerous things in it.
An ox accounted innocent, not previously testified against. Its owner pays half damages, from the value of the ox itself, so he never pays more than the ox is worth.
An ox that has been testified against. Its owner pays full damages from the best of his land. A human being is always an attested danger.
The payment for the harm done: half for a harmless animal, the whole for an attested danger or a person.
The duty of the one who wants payment to bring positive proof. Without it the defendant is found exempt.

debates.title: Does intention matter for a jug that breaks in the public domain?
debates.a: The first view: he is liable for the injury, with no distinction (Kulp: evidently they hold he is obligated even if it broke accidentally).
debates.b: Rabbi Judah: only if he broke it with intention; without intention he is not liable.

debates.title: Does Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel disagree with the first view?
debates.a: The first view: the one who put out the straw is liable for injuries, and whoever comes first may take it.
debates.b: Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel: whoever leaves disruptive things in the public domain must make restitution if they cause damage, and whoever comes first may take them. Kulp asks whether there is a disagreement at all.

debates.title: What does a harmless ox owe for hurting a man?
debates.a: The first view: the ox's owner pays only half damages.
debates.b: Rabbi Akiva: even a harmless ox that hurt a man pays full damages for the greater hurt.

debates.title: How is Exodus 21:35 applied?
debates.a: Rabbi Meir: with two oxen worth 200 and a worthless carcass, sell the live ox and divide its price.
debates.b: Rabbi Judah: that is the halakhah, but it fulfils only half the verse. The verse speaks of selling the live ox and also dividing the dead animal, as when the carcass is worth 50.
